paras: The shooting of John Grayson took place in Abingdon, Virginia, on the evening of Saturday, July 21, 1888, when Grayson, who had just shot a local man named Lilburn Trigg, was hit by a pistol ball fired by an unidentified person as a crowd chased him. Grayson died the next morning, Trigg three days later, and Trigg's mother of shock that night, and newspapers called it a triple tragedy. The Richmond Dispatch's Abingdon correspondent wrote that Grayson would have been lynched had he survived.

Grayson was in town with his uncle and others from his neighborhood, which the Richmond Dispatch gave as Johnson County, Tennessee, and the Alexandria Gazette as Cut Laurel Gap. The Staunton Spectator later described him as 22, the son of a Col. Jas. Grayson of Tennessee, who had brought a wagon-load of whiskey to town.

After drinking, Grayson started home on horseback with a companion; in front of the colored Methodist Episcopal church on Main Street he fired a pistol in the air and turned it toward the companion, according to the Dispatch. Lilburn Trigg, whom the Dispatch called a citizen and the Gazette a policeman, laid a hand on Grayson's shoulder and told him not to shoot. Grayson fired into Trigg's left shoulder, and Trigg fell, dragging Grayson off his horse.

As Grayson ran, amid cries of "Catch the murderer" and "Stop him" from a large crowd, a second shot was heard in the direction of his flight. Trigg's father, a constable, came out to arrest him and called on Samuel Mothner, a storekeeper, who tripped Grayson and took his pistol; only then was it found that Grayson had been shot in the back. The Gazette said he was fired on by someone near the scene, and the Spectator that "some one unknown" fired. Trigg's mother, seeing her son carried home apparently dead, died about one o'clock that night, and Grayson died by five the next morning.

Lilburn Trigg died on July 24, and the Dispatch reported that Grayson's mother was gravely ill from the news of her son's death. The correspondent wrote that it was not certainly known who shot Grayson, and that the general view was that the shot "only saved him from a more ignominious ending." No report of an inquest or of any charge against the person who shot Grayson appears in the coverage.

Virginia papers carried the story first: a paragraph in the Alexandria Gazette on July 23 and a long special telegram in the Richmond Dispatch on July 24 headed "A Sad Tragedy," with the deck "A Pistol-Ball Prevents a Lynching." The Gazette paragraph was reprinted in the Staunton Spectator, the Shenandoah Herald and the Clinch Valley News.

Outside Virginia, a Bristol dispatch of July 25 ran in the San Antonio Daily Light, the Memphis Appeal, both Wheeling dailies and the Middleburgh Post. It named the wounded man Lewis Trigg and said Grayson "fell to the road dead"; the Wheeling papers headed it "Avenged His Son," suggesting that the father fired the shot, which the text did not say. A Knoxville dispatch had Grayson "attacked by infuriated citizens and beaten" to death, and a Georgia paper used that version as a temperance lesson about "one drunk man."

In August a feature headed "Triple Tragedy" and "Sad Consequences of a Tennessee Desperado's Drunken Frenzy" ran in the Peninsula Enterprise, the Abbeville Press and Banner and the Fisherman & Farmer. It called Grayson a "ruffian" and an "infuriated assassin" and added "Hang him!" to the crowd's cries. Brief national summaries called it a quarrel in which both men were fatally shot, and no report gave the race of anyone involved.

The Abingdon telegrams placed the shooting on Saturday evening, while the Bristol dispatch dated it July 24 and the Durham Recorder "Monday." Accounts of Grayson's death also differed: shot by an unknown person and dying the next morning in the Virginia papers, "finally shot down" by an angry crowd in the Durham Recorder, killed on the spot in the Bristol dispatch, and beaten to death in the Knoxville dispatch. The Dispatch's local telegram, the most detailed account, describes the shot as fired by an unknown person and the lynching as averted.

reader.title: Shooting of John Grayson
bases: Grayson, fleeing after shooting Trigg, was shot by an unidentified person while a crowd chased him with cries to catch him (A1, A2, A8), and the Richmond correspondent wrote that he would have been lynched had he lived (A2); one version has the crowd shooting him down (A16) and another has citizens beating him to death (A11).

Independent Abingdon telegrams (A1, A2), the Bristol wire (A8) and the Knoxville wire (A11) agree that Grayson shot Trigg, fled from a pursuing crowd and died of injuries received in the pursuit, though they differ on how.

accounts.label: Abingdon special telegram (Richmond Dispatch)
accounts.gist: Amid cries of 'Catch the murderer' a shot was heard; Grayson was tripped by Mothner and found shot in the back; who shot him is not certainly known, and he would have been lynched had he lived.

accounts.label: Virginia news paragraph
accounts.gist: Grayson ran and was fired on by someone near the scene, the ball striking him in the back.

accounts.label: Bristol wire
accounts.gist: Grayson fled pursued by an 'excited mob'; as Trigg's constable father came out a shot was heard and Grayson fell dead in the road.

accounts.label: Durham Recorder condensation
accounts.gist: Grayson fled, followed by an angry crowd, and was finally shot down.

accounts.label: Knoxville wire
accounts.gist: Grayson was attacked by infuriated citizens and beaten so badly that he died.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headlined 'A Sad Tragedy' with 'A Pistol-Ball Prevents a Lynching', called Grayson 'desperate' and the averted lynching 'a more ignominious ending' without comment for or against.
The Bristol wire ran as 'Avenged His Son' and 'A Drunken Murderer', calling Grayson 'the murderer'.
The 'Triple Tragedy' feature called Grayson a 'Tennessee desperado', 'ruffian' and 'infuriated assassin' and reported the crowd's 'Hang him!' without disapproval.
A Georgia paper used the case as a temperance lesson on the grief 'one drunk man' can cause.
